g.title: Present simple and continuous; action and non-action verbs
g.rule:
Choose the tense by asking: is it always true / a habit, or is it happening now / temporary?

habits and facts → present simpleI usually cook at home. · She doesn't eat meat.
now or temporary → present continuousI'm cooking dinner now. · He's eating less sugar this month.
non-action verbs (like, know, want, need, prefer) → simple onlyI want a coffee. I'm wanting

Some verbs change meaning: I have two brothers (possess) but I'm having lunch (action).

ex.q: My sister ___ fish. She never eats it.
Be quiet, please. I ___ to the recipe.
This soup ___ delicious!
We ___ (not / usually / eat) out during the week.

talk: What do you usually eat on a normal weekday?
Are you trying to change anything about your diet at the moment?

l.intro: Two flatmates decide what to cook tonight.

script.t: Tom, what do you usually cook when it's your turn?
Usually something quick. Fried chicken, or grilled salmon if I have time.
I'm trying to cut down on fried food at the moment.
Fine. What about steamed fish with boiled rice and cabbage?
That sounds healthy, but a bit boring. Do we have anything spicy?
There's a tin of tomatoes and some fresh chillies. I'm thinking of making a spicy prawn curry.
Prawns? I don't eat them. I prefer beef or lamb.
OK, lamb curry then. I'm just checking the freezer. Yes, we have frozen lamb.
Great. And I'm making a cucumber and avocado salad right now.
Perfect. Raspberries for dessert?
I never say no to raspberries.

ex.q: What does Tom usually cook?
Aliya wants to eat more fried food.
Why don't they make prawn curry?
What is Aliya making?

lessons.title: Present simple and continuous; action and non-action verbs

g.title: Future forms: be going to, present continuous, will
g.rule:
English has no single future tense. Choose the form by the kind of future.

a plan or intention → be going toI'm going to visit my grandparents this summer.
a fixed arrangement (time, place) → present continuousWe're meeting my cousins at six.
a decision now, an offer, a promise, a prediction → willI'll help you. · I think he'll be a good father.

Use be going to for a prediction you can see: Look at those clouds — it's going to rain.

ex.q: “The phone is ringing.” “OK, I ___ it.”
My brother ___ married in June. They booked the restaurant last week.
I've decided. I ___ more time with my family this year.
I promise I ___ (not / tell) Mum.

talk: What are you doing with your family or friends this weekend?
How do you think families will be different in twenty years?

l.intro: Dana tells a colleague about her cousin's wedding next month.

script.t: Marat, I'm going to my cousin's wedding next month. The whole extended family will be there.
How many people is that?
About eighty. My great-grandfather is coming too. He's ninety-four.
Wow. Are you looking forward to it?
Mostly. My brother-in-law is quite bossy, and my little sister is going to be moody because she hates dresses.
And who is organising everything?
My stepmother. She's very reliable, so I think it'll be perfect.
Are you taking anybody?
No, I'm going alone. My cousin is an only child, so I'm helping her with everything.
That's kind. I'm sure she'll be grateful.
I hope so. I'll send you a photo.

ex.q: How many people will be at the wedding?
Who is organising the wedding?
Dana's cousin has two brothers.
How does Dana describe her brother-in-law?

lessons.title: Future forms: be going to, present continuous, will

g.title: Present perfect and past simple
g.rule:
Both talk about the past. The question is: do we say when?

experience or news, no time given → present perfectI've bought a new phone. · Have you ever lent money to a friend?
a finished time (yesterday, last year, in 2020) → past simpleI bought it last week. It cost a lot.
just / already / yet → present perfectShe's already paid. · I haven't saved enough yet.

Conversations often start in the present perfect and continue in the past simple: “Have you ever wasted money?” “Yes, I bought a guitar and never played it.”

ex.q: I ___ my wallet yesterday.
___ you ever ___ anything online and regretted it?
We haven't paid the bill ___.
She ___ (already / spend) all her money.

talk: Have you ever bought something you never used? What happened?
Are you a spender or a saver? Give an example.

l.intro: A brother asks his sister for help with money.

script.t: Saule, could you lend me twenty thousand until Friday?
Again? You still owe me ten thousand from last month.
I know, sorry. I've spent everything. I've just paid my phone bill and my insurance.
Have you ever tried to make a budget?
I made one in January, but I didn't follow it.
What did you waste your money on this time?
I bought new headphones last weekend. They cost a lot, but they're worth it.
Arman, you can't afford them! Have you saved anything this year?
Not yet. But I've opened a savings account.
Good. OK, I'll lend you the money, but I want it back on Friday.
Thank you. I promise I'll pay you back.

ex.q: How much does Arman already owe his sister?
What did Arman buy last weekend?
Arman followed his budget.
What does Saule decide?
o: To open an account for him

lessons.title: Listening: Can you lend me some money?

g.title: Present perfect + for / since; present perfect continuous
g.rule:
Use these forms for something that started in the past and is still true now.

for + a period · since + a starting pointI've lived here for three years / since 2022.
action verbs → present perfect continuous (have been + -ing)She's been working for a charity since May.
non-action verbs (know, be, have) → present perfect simpleWe've known each other for ages.

The continuous form is also used for a recent activity with a visible result: You look tired. Have you been running?

ex.q: How long ___ English?
I've had this job ___ last September.
They ___ each other since school.
He ___ (work) as a volunteer for two years.

talk: What have you been doing recently that is new for you?
Tell us about something you have had or done for a long time.

l.intro: A radio presenter talks to a volunteer who has changed her life.

script.t: Kamila, how long have you been running?
For three years. Before that I was always exhausted after ten minutes.
And you've been raising money for a children's charity. How did that start?
A friend asked me to help at a bake sale. I was amazed how much money we made.
How much have you raised so far?
Nearly two million tenge. People have been incredibly positive.
What has been the most difficult moment?
Last winter I ran twenty kilometres. It was freezing and I was starving at the end.
But you finished?
Yes, and I was delighted. A local company has sponsored me since then.
That's a fascinating story. I hope you inspire our listeners.

ex.q: How long has Kamila been running?
What first got her into fundraising?
The weather was hot during her twenty-kilometre run.
Who has sponsored her?

g.title: Comparatives and superlatives
g.rule:
Compare two things with a comparative; pick one from a group with a superlative.

short adjectivesfast → faster → the fastest
long adjectivescomfortable → more comfortable → the most comfortable
the same / not the sameThe bus is as quick as the tram. · It isn't as cheap as the train.
adverbsShe drives more carefully than me.

Irregular: good → better → the best · bad → worse → the worst · far → further → the furthest.

ex.q: Cycling is ___ than driving in the city centre.
It's ___ journey I've ever made.
The metro isn't ___ the bus.
Trains are ___ (comfortable) than buses.

talk: What is the best way to travel around your city? Compare two ways.
Describe the longest or worst journey you have ever made.

l.intro: Two colleagues compare how they travel to the office.

script.t: Ben, you're early! Did you come by car?
No, by scooter. It's much quicker than driving in the rush hour.
Really? I set off at seven thirty and I was in a traffic jam for forty minutes.
The motorway is the worst place at that time. There are road works too.
I know. Is the tram better?
It's slower than the scooter, but it's the most relaxing way to travel.
And it's cheaper than petrol. I paid a parking fine last week as well.
Why don't you cycle? There's a new cycle lane along the river.
It isn't as safe as people say. Drivers don't always stop at the zebra crossing.
True. Then try the tram tomorrow and tell me which is best.
OK. I'll pick up a ticket tonight.

ex.q: How did Ben travel to work?
How long was Aigerim in the traffic jam?
Ben thinks the tram is the most relaxing way to travel.
What will Aigerim do tomorrow?

g.title: Articles: a / an, the, no article
g.rule:
Ask: is it new information, known information, or things in general?

we know which one, only one, superlatives → theThe man was tall. · the sun · the best

places: home, work, school, bedShe's at work. · He goes to school by bus.

ex.q: ___ teenagers spend a lot of time online.
My mother is ___ doctor.
Could you close ___ door, please?

talk: Is it true that men and women talk about different things? What do you think?
Describe a stereotype about your country that is wrong.

l.intro: Two parents talk in a toy shop.

script.t: Timur, are you looking for a present?
Yes, for my daughter. She's keen on construction toys, but the shop puts them in the boys' section.
That's a stereotype. My son loves soft toys and nobody laughs at him.
Exactly. I don't want to generalize, but adverts are full of prejudice.
The dolls are always pink and the toy vehicles are always blue.
And children choose between them because of the colour, not the toy.
Do you think it's harmful?
A little. Children depend on adults to show them that everything is possible.
I agree. What are you going to buy?
A construction set and dressing-up clothes. She's proud of the things she builds.
Good choice. I'm tired of pink boxes too.

ex.q: What does Timur's daughter like?
Laura's son is laughed at because of his toys.
According to the speakers, why do children choose a toy?
What is Timur going to buy?

g.title: Obligation and prohibition: have to, must, should
g.rule:
These verbs show how strong a rule or piece of advice is.

a rule or necessity → have to / mustYou have to switch off your phone. · You must be on time.
not necessary → don't have toYou don't have to bring a present.
prohibited → mustn'tYou mustn't speak loudly here.
advice or opinion → should / shouldn'tYou should say thank you.

Careful: don't have to (your choice) is very different from mustn't (don't do it!).

ex.q: It's a free concert. You ___ pay.
You ___ use your phone during the exam. It's forbidden.
I think you ___ apologise to her.
In my last job I ___ (have to) wear a suit.

talk: What are three rules of good manners in your country?
What should people never do with their phones? Why?

l.intro: A mother and her teenage son disagree about phone manners.

script.t: Daniel, you shouldn't scroll through your phone at dinner.
I'm not scrolling, Mum. I'm reading one notification.
You have to switch it off, or at least put it on silent mode.
But I must reply to this message. It's about homework.
You don't have to answer immediately. Your friend can wait twenty minutes.
What if someone calls?
Then you can call back later. Yesterday your ringtone went off three times.
OK, but Dad mustn't take selfies with his food then.
That's fair. The rule is for everybody.
Fine. I'll mute it. But you should stop sending me voice notes from the kitchen.
Agreed. Now pass the salad, please.

ex.q: What is Daniel doing at the table?
Daniel's mother says he must answer immediately.
How many times did his ringtone go off yesterday?
What does Daniel ask his mother to stop doing?

lessons.title: Obligation and prohibition: have to, must, should

g.title: Ability and possibility: can, could, be able to
g.rule:
Can has only two forms (can, could). Use be able to for all the others.

present · pastI can swim. · I could read when I was four.
futureI'll be able to drive next year.
present perfectI've never been able to dance.
after another verb or toI'd love to be able to speak Chinese.

For one successful moment in the past, say was able to or managed to: The test was hard, but I was able to finish it.

ex.q: I'd like to ___ play the piano.
She ___ speak three languages when she was ten.
I've never ___ cook well.
After this course you ___ (be able to) understand films in English.

talk: What is something you could not do before but can do now? How did you learn it?
What would you love to be able to do?

l.intro: An interviewer talks to a man who learned Spanish as an adult.

script.t: Erlan, could you speak any Spanish two years ago?
No, I couldn't say a word. I was embarrassed to try.
And now you're able to have a conversation. What changed?
I found a teacher who gave me useful feedback. Before that, lessons were boring.
Were you ever frustrated?
Often. It's frustrating when you can understand but you can't answer quickly.
What was the most exciting moment?
Last summer in Madrid I was able to order dinner and chat to the waiter. I was amazed.
Would you like to be able to speak more languages?
Yes. I'll never be a polyglot, but I'd love to be able to read Italian.
I'm sure you'll be able to. Thank you, Erlan.

ex.q: Erlan could speak some Spanish two years ago.
Why were his first lessons a problem?
What did he manage to do in Madrid?
What would he love to be able to do next?

lessons.title: Ability and possibility: can, could, be able to
Listening: Learning a language at fifty

g.title: Past and present habits: used to, usually

g.title: Modals of deduction: might, can't, must

Use these modals to say how sure you are about something.

g.title: Third conditional
g.rule:
Use the third conditional to imagine a different past. It cannot change now.

if + past perfect, would have + past participleIf I had left earlier, I would have caught the train.
negativeIf she hadn't helped me, I wouldn't have passed.
short formsIf I'd known, I'd have told you.

ex.q: If I ___ the map, I wouldn't have got lost.
We ___ the flight if the taxi had come on time.
If you had asked me, I ___ you.
If he ___ (not / stop) to help, they would never have met.

talk: Describe a lucky or unlucky moment in your life. What would have happened if things had been different?
Do you believe in luck? Why or why not?

l.intro: Two friends talk about a missed flight.

script.t: Asel, how was your trip?
Strange. I missed my flight because the taxi was delayed.
How unlucky!
Actually, it was lucky. If I had caught that flight, I wouldn't have met my new business partner.
What do you mean?
I had to stay in a hostel near the airport. A stranger there helped me with my bags.
And?
We started talking. If she hadn't been so kind, I would never have told her about my idea.
And she liked it?
She loved it. We signed an agreement last week.
So if the taxi had arrived on time, nothing would have happened.
Exactly. Sometimes a problem is an opportunity.

ex.q: Why did Asel miss her flight?
Where did she stay?
Asel thinks missing the flight was bad luck.
Who did she meet?

g.title: Quantifiers
g.rule:
Quantifiers say how much or how many.

large amountsa lot of / lots of apps · plenty of time
small amountsa few messages (countable) · a little time (uncountable)
more than you want · less than you needtoo much noise · too many emails · not enough sleep
zeroThere's no signal. · There aren't any sockets.

Enough goes before a noun but after an adjective: enough money · fast enough.

ex.q: I spend ___ time on my phone.
There are only ___ people who don't use the internet.
My laptop isn't ___.
I get too ___ emails every day.

talk: How much time do you spend on screens every day? Is it too much?
Which app or device could you not live without?

l.intro: A grandfather asks his granddaughter for help with technology.

script.t: Lena, nothing works in this house. There are too many remote controls.
How many do you have?
Four. And none of them switches on the television.
Have you plugged it in? There isn't any light on the socket.
Oh. No, I unplugged it to charge my phone.
You don't have enough sockets. You need an adaptor.
And the printer doesn't print. I've wasted a lot of paper.
You need to install an update. It only takes a few minutes.
I spend too much time on these machines.
Do you use the voice assistant?
A little. It never understands me. I turn it down.
Let me help. There, everything works. Just don't delete anything.

ex.q: How many remote controls does Grandpa have?
Why didn't the television work?
The printer needs an update.
What does Lena tell him not to do?

g.title: Relative clauses: defining and non-defining
g.rule:
A relative clause gives information about a person, thing or place.

necessary information (defining): who / which / that / where / whoseShe's the woman who started the company.
extra information (non-defining): commas, no thatThe founder, who was born in Almaty, is now famous.
places and possessionthe city where I grew up · the man whose idea changed the world

ex.q: He's the designer ___ created the logo.
This is the building ___ my father works.
My phone, ___ I bought last year, is already broken.
She's the writer ___ books I love.

talk: Describe a person you admire: who are they, and what have they done?
Describe an object that is important to you.

l.intro: A student gives a short talk and a classmate asks questions.

script.t: The person I admire most is my aunt, who is a fashion designer.
Is she the one whose shop is in the old shopping street?
Yes. It's the shop where I worked last summer.
What's her greatest achievement?
She designed the clothes that our national team wore last year.
Is she famous?
She's quite influential, but fame isn't something that interests her.
What is she like?
She's talented and ambitious, which is why she works so hard.
Has anyone written about her?
A journalist who interviewed her is writing her biography.
She sounds like a real hero. Thanks, Zhanna.

ex.q: What is Zhanna's aunt's job?
What did she design last year?
Zhanna's aunt is very interested in fame.
Who is writing her biography?

g.title: Question tags
g.rule:
Add a question tag to check information or to ask someone to agree.

positive sentence → negative tagYou're a detective, aren't you?
negative sentence → positive tagShe didn't see him, did she?
use the same auxiliaryThey've left, haven't they? · He can drive, can't he?
no auxiliary → do / does / didYou live here, don't you?

ex.q: You were at home last night, ___?
She doesn't know him, ___?
They've arrested someone, ___?
It was a difficult case, ___ it?

talk: Describe a crime story, film or series you know. What happened?
Would you be a good detective? Why or why not?

l.intro: An inspector questions a witness about a robbery.

script.t: Mrs Karimova, you live opposite the jewellery shop, don't you?
Yes, I do. I've lived there for twenty years.
You were at home last night, weren't you?
I was. I was watching television.
You heard a noise at about eleven, didn't you?
That's right. I looked out and saw a man with a bag.
You couldn't see his face, could you?
No, but he was tall, and he got into a white van.
You haven't seen that van before, have you?
Actually, I have. It was parked there on Monday too.
That's an important clue. You'd recognise it again, wouldn't you?
I think so. I even wrote down part of the number.

ex.q: Where does Mrs Karimova live?
What time did she hear a noise?
She saw the man's face clearly.
What important clue does she give?
o: The van was there on Monday too
